notes.h: The waste hierarchy and sustainable waste management
notes.b: Sustainable waste management means reducing waste first, then reusing, recycling and recovering value, and disposing of only what is left. The waste hierarchy ranks the options from most to least preferred, so that as little waste as possible reaches disposal.
points: The order of preference is prevention, minimisation, reuse, recycling, recovery (including energy recovery) and disposal. Marking schemes phrase it as reduce, reuse, recycle, recover, dispose.
Prevention and minimisation come first: buying only what is needed and avoiding excess packaging stops waste being created in the first place, so there is nothing to collect or treat.

Reuse means using an item again for its original or another purpose, such as refilling a container, reusing a jar for storage, repairing, donating or buying second-hand. The item stays whole, which is why reuse is not recycling.
Recycling processes used materials into new products, such as paper, glass, metals, some plastics and textiles. It saves raw materials and usually energy, and keeps waste out of landfill.

Recovery means burning residual waste to generate heat or electricity (energy from waste); gas collected from landfill can also be used for energy. Energy recovery is not recycling, because the material is not made into a new product.

Disposal, mainly landfill, is the least preferred option because it uses up land, and food and other organic waste decomposes without oxygen (anaerobically), releasing methane, a potent greenhouse gas.

In Irish law the hierarchy is applied through the Waste Management Act 1996 (as amended). It sets up controls on waste collection and movement, and gives local authorities and the EPA roles in promoting waste reduction, recycling and reuse.
notes.tip: When asked how consumers contribute to sustainable waste management, give two separate points such as reduce, reuse, recycle, compost, buy in bulk, buy recyclable products or concentrated detergents. Do not mix up reuse (item kept whole), recycling (broken down into new products) and energy recovery.

notes.b: Much household waste is biodegradable, meaning it can be rotted down by living things. Composting turns it into something useful instead of sending it to landfill.
points: Biodegradable material such as food scraps, tea leaves and garden waste is broken down by micro-organisms into a nutrient-rich soil conditioner called compost. Composting differs from recycling because organic matter rots down rather than being reprocessed into a new product.
Composting keeps biodegradable waste out of landfill, so less methane is produced as it would otherwise rot without oxygen.
Compost returns nutrients and organic matter to the soil, so gardeners need less peat-based compost, and it is cheap for households to make.

In Irish households food and garden waste is collected in the brown bin where a collection is provided. The three bins are green (dry recyclables), brown (food and garden waste) and black (general waste).
notes.tip: Say that micro-organisms break the waste down, and give two benefits, such as less methane from landfill and nutrients returned to the soil.

notes.b: Most waste can be cut at home by what a household buys and how it sorts what is left. Each action below moves waste up the hierarchy, away from disposal.
points: Plan meals and write a shopping list, so food is not bought and then thrown away.
Buy concentrated products, such as concentrated detergents, which need less packaging per wash. Buy in bulk where it cuts packaging per unit, and use refill stations and refillable containers.
Use reusable bags, bottles and containers instead of single-use ones, so fewer items are made and thrown away. Reuse jars, tubs and shopping bags.
Separate waste at home into recyclables, food and garden waste, and general waste, so that each stream can be treated in the right way.
Choose products in recyclable, recycled or biodegradable packaging, and products with the EU Ecolabel. Repair items rather than replacing them.

Take paint and other household chemicals to a civic amenity site (the local authority's recycling and waste centre), not the bin, because they can harm the environment and the people handling waste. Do not put paint, oil, chemicals or batteries in the bin.
notes.tip: For ways to reduce waste when shopping for food, give specific actions: refuse excess packaging, choose loose produce, bring reusable bags, choose recyclable or biodegradable packaging, use refill and bulk buying.

notes.b: Packaging carries symbols that tell the consumer how it can be treated after use. The recycling symbol is the most common, and it says less than many people think.
points: The recycling symbol (three arrows forming a loop) shows that the packaging is made of material that can be recycled. It does not guarantee that a local collection accepts it, so do not say it is certainly accepted in the household recycling bin.
A percentage inside the arrows shows the proportion of recycled content in the packaging.
A number inside a triangle on plastic is a plastic-type code: 1 is PET, used for drinks bottles, and 2 is HDPE, used for milk bottles and detergent containers.
notes.tip: If asked what the recycling symbol tells you, answer that the packaging contains recyclable material. Do not mix up the recycling loop, the Green Dot and the Ecolabel in one answer.

notes.b: Two other symbols are often confused with the recycling loop. They tell the consumer about who paid for recovery and about a product's whole environmental effect, not whether the pack can be recycled.
points: The Green Dot shows that the producer of the packaging has contributed financially to the recovery and recycling of packaging waste.
In Ireland the Green Dot is shown by members of Repak, the packaging recovery scheme, so a producer who pays into Repak can put it on their packs.
The Green Dot does not mean the item itself is recyclable or recycled, which is why it must not be treated as a recycling symbol.
The EU Ecolabel, a flower symbol, is an audited, voluntary label certifying that a product or service causes minimum damage to the environment across its life cycle.
The Ecolabel assessment considers the energy and materials used in making the product, the pollution produced, and how far it can be reused or recycled.
notes.tip: For the Green Dot, say the producer has paid towards recovery and recycling of packaging, and name Repak for Ireland. For the Ecolabel, say minimum damage to the environment, judged over the product's life.

notes.b: Packaging makes up a large share of household waste, so government, producers, local authorities and consumers all act to reduce it. A strong answer names one initiative and gives two details about it.
points: The levy on single-use plastic shopping bags, charged at the point of sale since 2002, discouraged their use and increased the use of reusable bags.
The landfill levy is a charge per tonne on waste sent to landfill, which makes landfill more expensive and so encourages recycling and recovery.
Packaging producers must meet national recovery and recycling targets under Irish packaging regulations, and most meet them by funding the Repak scheme (the Green Dot).
Local authority recycling schemes gather glass, cans, paper and plastics through kerbside collections and bring banks or civic amenity centres.

The Re-turn deposit return scheme began on 1 February 2024. A refundable deposit is paid on plastic drinks bottles and aluminium and steel cans, which are returned in shops or to reverse vending machines. Glass and dairy containers are not included.
Consumers can refuse over-packaged goods, choose loose produce and bring their own containers to refill counters.
Manufacturers reduce excess packaging by using less material per product and lighter packaging.
notes.tip: When asked for one initiative to reduce the effect of packaging, name it (plastic bag levy, landfill levy, local authority recycling, deposit return, Green Dot, WEEE or Ecolabel) and then give two details for the marks.

notes.b: Each packaging material has strengths for the product and a different fate as waste. Knowing both lets you judge how sustainable a material is.
points: Flexible films are thin plastic films that are light, low in cost, fit the shape of the food closely, can be printed on and can be heat-sealed (closed by melting the edges together).
Flexible films give a good barrier against moisture and gases, which extends shelf life and reduces spoilage, and they are suitable for frozen food.
Their drawback is that many multi-layer films are hard to recycle, so they are often sent to landfill or energy recovery.
Glass can be washed and reused, or recycled repeatedly without loss of quality, but it is heavy and costly to transport.
Steel and aluminium cans are highly recyclable, and aluminium can be recycled repeatedly without loss of quality.
Paper and card are recyclable, though their fibres shorten with each recycling cycle. They also come from a renewable raw material, are biodegradable, are light and take printing well.
Biodegradable packaging breaks down naturally through the action of micro-organisms. Examples are paper or card, and compostable starch-based packaging.
notes.tip: For two advantages of flexible films, choose from cost, barrier to moisture and gases, heat sealing, close fit to the shape of the food, light weight, printing and suitability for frozen food. For biodegradable packaging, explain the micro-organisms and give an example.

notes.b: WEEE is waste electrical and electronic equipment, and it is governed by its own collection and take-back rules. It must be kept out of the general bin because of what it contains.
points: Electrical goods contain hazardous substances such as lead, mercury, cadmium and brominated flame retardants, and also valuable materials that can be recovered, so they must not go into general household waste.
The crossed-out wheeled bin symbol means the item must be collected separately from household waste.
Route 1: repair, sell or donate a working appliance first, because keeping it in use is the top of the waste hierarchy.
Route 2: when a consumer buys a new equivalent item, the retailer must take back the old one free of charge, including on home delivery.

Route 3: a civic amenity site or recycling centre accepts small appliances, batteries and other electrical items. Larger electrical shops must accept very small electrical items without a purchase, and batteries can be returned to shops without buying anything.
Take batteries out of appliances and dispose of them separately before the appliance is handed in. Erase personal data from smart appliances.
Old fridges and freezers contain refrigerant and insulating foam, which must be removed by an authorised treatment facility. Make the appliance safe before disposal.
The legal basis is the WEEE Directive, applied in Ireland by the European Union (Waste Electrical and Electronic Equipment) Regulations 2014.
notes.tip: When asked how to dispose of electrical appliances, three separate routes earn three separate marks: retailer take-back, civic amenity or recycling centre, and repair or donate first. Mention batteries out and special care with fridges.

keyTerms.definition: Managing waste so that it is reduced, reused, recycled or recovered before any remainder is disposed of.
A ranking of waste options from most to least preferred: prevention, minimisation, reuse, recycling, recovery and disposal.
Able to be broken down by micro-organisms into natural substances.
The controlled breakdown of biodegradable waste by micro-organisms into a soil conditioner.
The disposal of waste by burying it in the ground, where organic waste decomposes and releases methane.
Processing used materials into new products so that they do not go to waste.
A symbol showing that the packaging producer has contributed financially to packaging recovery and recycling.
A flower symbol awarded to products and services that cause minimum environmental damage over their life cycle.
A thin, light plastic packaging film that closely fits the food it wraps and acts as a barrier to moisture and gases.
Waste electrical and electronic equipment, which must be collected and treated separately from general household waste.

factCards.term: Six stages of the waste hierarchy
factCards.definition: Prevention, minimisation, reuse, recycling, recovery and disposal, in order of preference.

factCards.term: Four consumer actions to reduce packaging waste
factCards.definition: Buy concentrated products; choose loose produce; refuse over-packaged goods; bring reusable bags and containers.
That the packaging producer has contributed financially to packaging recovery and recycling; it does not show that the packaging itself is recyclable.
It keeps food and garden waste out of landfill and so reduces methane; it returns nutrients to the soil; it reduces the need for peat-based compost.

factCards.term: Four hazardous substances in electrical goods
factCards.definition: Lead, mercury, cadmium and brominated flame retardants.
Low cost, a good barrier against moisture and gases, and suitability for heat sealing and frozen food.

factCards.term: Three pieces of information on a recycling symbol
factCards.definition: Whether the item is made of recyclable material; the recycled content as a percentage; the plastic type as a number inside the triangle.

factCards.term: Two steps before disposing of an old fridge
factCards.definition: Make the appliance safe, and let an authorised facility remove refrigerant and foam.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between recycling and composting as ways of managing household waste, and give one example of a material suited to each.
questions.model: Recycling: used materials are processed into new products, so the material itself is reused in manufacture; example: glass bottles or aluminium cans. Composting: biodegradable material is broken down by micro-organisms into a soil conditioner rather than being manufactured again; example: fruit and vegetable peelings or garden waste. Full marks need the process named for each method and a suitable example for each.

questions.prompt: Discuss how consumers can reduce the excess packaging they bring into the home. Describe what the Green Dot and the EU Ecolabel indicate to the consumer, and explain how an old electrical appliance should be disposed of.
questions.model: Packaging reduction: buy concentrated products; choose loose produce; buy in bulk where packaging per unit is lower; refuse over-packaged goods; bring reusable bags and containers. Green Dot: the producer has contributed financially to packaging recovery and recycling; it does not show that the item is recyclable. EU Ecolabel: the product or service causes minimum environmental damage over its life cycle, considering manufacturing energy and materials, pollution and reusability. Disposal of electrical appliances: keep them out of household bins because they contain hazardous substances; return them to a retailer, which must take back an equivalent old item when a new one is bought, or to a local authority recycling centre; remove batteries and, for fridges and freezers, the doors; older units must go to an authorised treatment facility to remove refrigerant and foam.
